displayQuote: Anyone who is not shocked by quantum theory has not understood it

meta.title: Who really said "Anyone who is not shocked by quantum theory has not understood it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Bohr never wrote it. Heisenberg recalled Bohr saying something close (Physics and Beyond, 1971); this short wording is in print by 1981.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Anyone who is not shocked by quantum theory has not understood it'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Bohr's written words: a later paraphrase of remarks Heisenberg and Frisch remembered him making. The short form is in print by 1981.

answer.label: Not Niels Bohr’s words — a later paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: Bohr never wrote this sentence. The idea comes from colleagues’ memories of what he said. Werner Heisenberg recalled Bohr saying that “those who are not shocked when they first come across quantum theory cannot possibly have understood it” (Physics and Beyond, 1971). Otto Frisch remembered a “giddy” version. The short “Anyone who is not shocked…” form is a later paraphrase, in print by 1981. Wikiquote ↗ lists it under “Disputed.”

source.excerpt: Those who are not shocked when they first come across quantum theory cannot possibly have understood it.
trail: 1967: A colleague’s memory appears in Stefan Rozental’s collection Niels Bohr: His Life and Work as Seen by His Friends and Colleagues (p. 139). In it, Bohr replies to someone who said the questions made him giddy: “that only shows he has not understood the first thing about them.” Otto Frisch tells the same story in What Little I Remember (1979), p. 95 (ADS-L, Garson O’Toole and Ben Zimmer ↗).

1971: Heisenberg’s Physics and Beyond (p. 206) has Bohr saying that those “not shocked when they first come across quantum theory cannot possibly have understood it.” Wikiquote also cites the German Der Teil und das Ganze (1969), p. 280 (Wikiquote ↗).

1981–1984: The short wording appears in print. Kit Pedler’s Mind over Matter (1981) introduces it with “Niels Bohr wrote,” and John Gribbin’s In Search of Schrödinger’s Cat (1984) uses it as an epigraph (ADS-L, Bill Mullins ↗).

Today: Wikiquote lists the exact wording under “Disputed.” It reproduces David Mermin’s report that he searched the three volumes of Bohr’s philosophical writings for remarks like this and found none (Wikiquote ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is Heisenberg’s memory of something Bohr said in conversation, not a sentence Bohr wrote. The page number is the one Wikiquote cites. The familiar “Anyone who is not shocked by quantum theory has not understood it” is a shorter rewording of it.

source.rightsNote: No single work is the source of the popular wording. It is an anonymous paraphrase, in print by 1981, so we make no public-domain claim. The remembered versions it grew from all come from 1931-or-later books: Rozental (1967), Heisenberg (1969 German; 1971 English) and Frisch (1979). Those are under copyright in their own right.

author.name: Niels Bohr

author.heading: About Niels Bohr
author.metaLine: 1885–1962 · Danish physicist, Nobel Prize in Physics 1922
author.bio: Niels Bohr (born in Copenhagen, 7 October 1885; died there 18 November 1962) won the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the structure of atoms. He led the Copenhagen institute now named after him, and he gave quantum theory the principle of complementarity. His published essays are famously careful and undramatic. Most of the striking one-liners credited to him come from colleagues’ memories, not from his own pen.

misattribution.heading: Where the attribution goes wrong
misattribution.intro: Bohr probably did say something like this. Two colleagues remembered versions of it. But the crisp sentence going around today is not his, and the claim that he wrote it has no support.

items.why: Kit Pedler’s Mind over Matter (1981) introduces the line with “Niels Bohr wrote” (ADS-L ↗). But David Mermin searched the three volumes of Bohr’s philosophical writings for remarks like this and “failed to turn up anything comparable” (Wikiquote ↗).

Karen Barad’s Meeting the Universe Halfway (2007) cites this collection for the line, but, as Wikiquote notes, gives no volume or page number. Ben Zimmer found no searchable copy of the collection to check it against (ADS-L ↗).

items.who: “Anyone who is not shocked by quantum theory has not understood it”
items.why: Heisenberg’s version is longer: “Those who are not shocked when they first come across quantum theory cannot possibly have understood it” (Wikiquote ↗). The short form is in print in 1981 and 1984. The Oxford Dictionary of Quotations gives a third version (“Anybody who is not shocked by this subject has failed to understand it”), citing Nature, 23 August 1990 (ADS-L ↗).

Otto Frisch remembered Bohr telling a visitor that anyone who could think about quantum theory “without getting giddy” had not “understood the first thing about it” (What Little I Remember, 1979, p. 95). The quote is also usually given in Danish with “dizzy” (svimmel), not “shocked” (ADS-L ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Bohr’s as his colleagues remembered it. The wording is not. Credit the familiar line as “attributed to Niels Bohr, paraphrasing Heisenberg’s account in Physics and Beyond (1971)” (Wikiquote ↗), not as something he wrote.

context.heading: Why the line sticks to Bohr
lead: Bohr was the central figure of the “Copenhagen” reading of quantum mechanics, and generations of physicists passed on stories about him. The “shocked” remark matches his insistence that quantum theory forces us to change how we describe nature. That fit made it an easy line to put in his mouth.

His own prose was nothing like it. When physicist David Mermin went looking for quotable lines in Bohr’s collected essays, he found careful, abstract sentences, not slogans. The memorable versions come from Heisenberg’s and Frisch’s memories, and the polished one-liner from later popular-science books.
context.detailsSummary: The remembered versions, side by side
detailsBody: Rozental (1967), p. 139: “But if anybody says he can think about quantum problems without getting giddy, that only shows he has not understood the first thing about them.” Ben Zimmer’s snippet-view search suggests the passage is part of Otto Robert Frisch’s remembrance (ADS-L ↗).

Heisenberg, Physics and Beyond (1971), p. 206: “Those who are not shocked when they first come across quantum theory cannot possibly have understood it.” Wikiquote places it in a 1952 conversation with Heisenberg and Pauli in Copenhagen (Wikiquote ↗).

Frisch, What Little I Remember (1979), p. 95: “if anybody says he can think about quantum theory without getting giddy it merely shows that he hasn’t understood the first thing about it!” Garson O’Toole checked this against the printed book (ADS-L ↗).
context.pull: Others attributed spectacular remarks to him, but he seemed to take pains to avoid any hint of the dramatic in his own writings. — David Mermin, as reproduced on Wikiquote

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Quotes section gives "Those who are not shocked when they first come across quantum theory cannot possibly have understood it," from a 1952 conversation with Heisenberg and Pauli, citing Heisenberg, Physics and Beyond (Harper & Row, 1971), p. 206.

Wikiquote lists the exact wording "Anyone who is not shocked by quantum theory has not understood it" under Disputed. It cites Der Teil und das Ganze (Piper, 1969), p. 280, notes that Barad (2007, p. 254) cites The Philosophical Writings of Niels Bohr with no page or volume, and reproduces Mermin's report that he found nothing comparable in Bohr's writings.

The ODQ gives "Anybody who is not shocked by this subject has failed to understand it," citing Nature, 23 August 1990. Pedler's Mind over Matter (Thames Methuen, 1981) has "Niels Bohr wrote: 'Anyone who is not shocked by quantum theory has not understood it.'" Gribbin's In Search of Schrodinger's Cat (1984) uses it as the epigraph on p. 5.

Frisch, What Little I Remember (Cambridge University Press, 1979), p. 95, checked on paper, has the giddy anecdote. Rozental (1967), p. 139, has "that only shows he has not understood the first thing about them," which Zimmer places within Frisch's remembrance.
Chris Waigl says the quote is usually given in Danish with 'svimmel' (dizzy) and advises against insisting on 'shocked'.
Ben Zimmer: Barad gives the 'shocked' version citing The Philosophical Writings of Niels Bohr, but he could not find a searchable copy to confirm it.
